ford-model-t: The Model T is the car that made owning a car normal. Ford’s moving assembly line cut build times and prices, so ordinary families could afford one. It was simple, tall on its wheels and easy to repair with basic tools, which suited the poor roads of its day. At a show, look at the pedals: they work very differently from a modern car, and drivers had to learn them before setting off.
volkswagen-beetle: The Beetle’s round shape and rear air-cooled engine made it one of the most recognisable cars ever built. It stayed in production for decades and sold in huge numbers around the world. Owners love its simple mechanics and the large supply of spare parts. If you are looking at one, check the floor pans and the heater channels for rust.
willys-mb-jeep: The Willys MB was built for the army, and its toughness is the reason the word jeep became a name for small off-road vehicles. It is light, narrow and very simple, with a flat bonnet and a folding windscreen. Restored examples are popular at shows and parts are well supported by specialists. Check the frame and body tub for hidden rust, as many were used hard.
morris-minor: The Minor was designed by Alec Issigonis, the same engineer who later created the Mini. It was small, cheap to run and pleasant to drive, so it became a family favourite in Britain and beyond. Its simple engine and mechanical parts are easy to maintain, which makes it a good first classic. Look for rust around the sills and the wings before you buy.
mercedes-benz-300-sl: The 300 SL is famous for its gullwing doors, which open upward because of the tubular frame underneath. It was one of the fastest road cars of its time and used fuel injection, which was advanced for the 1950s. Today it is a blue-chip collector car and very expensive. If you see one in person, notice how high and wide the door sills are, a direct result of that frame.
chevrolet-bel-air: The Bel Air became the face of 1950s American style, especially the 1955 to 1957 models with their chrome, bold colours and optional V8. It was sold as an ordinary family car, which is why so many survive and why parts are easy to find. Many owners enjoy modifying them. When buying, check for rust in the lower body and ask about any engine swaps.
citroen-ds: The DS looked like nothing else when it appeared in 1955. Its self-levelling hydropneumatic suspension gave a very smooth ride, and its smooth body was years ahead of its rivals. The car rises on its suspension after you start the engine, which surprises first-time viewers. It is complex, so a specialist mechanic is a must if you are thinking of buying one.
jaguar-e-type: Launched in 1961, the E-Type combined sports-car performance with a shape that many people still call one of the most beautiful ever drawn. Its long bonnet hides a straight-six engine, and it cost far less than rivals with similar speed. Early cars are the most sought-after. Check the bonnet and floor for rust and make sure the paperwork matches the car.
ford-mustang: The Mustang arrived in 1964 and created the pony car class: a stylish, affordable coupe with a long bonnet and a short rear. Buyers could pick a mild six-cylinder or a powerful V8, so it suited almost every budget. It was a huge sales success from the first year. Parts are easy to find, which makes it a friendly classic to own.
pontiac-gto: Many people credit the GTO with starting the muscle car era by fitting a large V8 into a mid-size Pontiac. The idea was simple, and the result was fast, loud and popular with young buyers. Genuine early cars are valuable and many look-alikes exist, so check the identification numbers carefully before paying for a real GTO.
dodge-charger: The Charger of the late 1960s is remembered for its bold grille, hidden headlights and big engines. It became a screen star as well, which keeps its popularity high. Engines ranged from modest to very powerful, and the value of a car depends heavily on which one it has. Always ask for proof of the original engine.
chevrolet-camaro: Chevrolet built the Camaro to compete with the Mustang, and it did so with sharp styling and a wide range of engines. The first generation, which ended in 1969, is the one most collectors chase. Many cars were modified over the years, so a car with its original parts is worth more. Check the front subframe and the rear spring mounts for rust.
porsche-911-classic: The early 911 kept its air-cooled engine at the back and its rounded shape for decades, which is why the car looks instantly familiar. It is a driver’s car, with light steering and a distinctive engine sound. Early models are valuable, and later air-cooled cars are rising in price too. Look for service records, because engine work can be costly.
hillman-hunter: The Hunter was a practical British family saloon designed to be simple and durable. It was built in several countries, and its sturdy build suited rough roads. Today it is a rare sight, which gives it a charm of its own at classic shows. Spare parts need patience to find, so joining an owners’ club is a good idea.
mercedes-benz-w123: The W123 earned a reputation for durability, and many are still working decades after they were built. Its upright shape, comfortable seats and strong diesel options made it a favourite as a taxi and a family car in many countries. Simple mechanics keep running costs fair. Rust in the wheel arches and sills is the main thing to check.
toyota-corolla-e100: The E100 Corolla is remembered for being easy to live with: comfortable, economical and very reliable. The Corolla name is one of the best known on the road in Pakistan, so this generation feels familiar to many drivers. It is a sensible choice for someone who wants a simple older car for daily use. Look for a clean service history and check the rear arches for rust.
suzuki-mehran: The Mehran was a small, light hatchback that carried countless families in Pakistan for over thirty years. It was cheap to buy and to repair, and parts were available almost everywhere. It was built with older technology and basic safety features, so keep that in mind if you plan to drive one regularly. It has a loyal following and is slowly becoming a nostalgic classic.
suzuki-alto: The Alto is a small car designed for city driving, with low running costs and an easy size to park. Over the years it has appeared in many versions in different countries, so details vary from place to place. It is popular with first-time buyers because it is simple to maintain. When looking at an older one, check the engine mounts and the interior, since small cars are often used hard.
bmw-3-series-e30: The E30 is the 3 Series that many enthusiasts love most: compact, balanced and satisfying to drive. It came in many forms, including saloons, convertibles and the famous M3. Clean examples are now rising in price. Check for rust around the rear arches and the boot floor, and look for signs that the car has been driven hard.
toyota-2000gt: The 2000GT proved that Japan could build a world-class sports car. It has a long bonnet, a low roof and a refined straight-six engine, and it was built in very small numbers. That rarity keeps prices very high today. It also appeared in a famous spy film, which added to its fame. Most people will only see one in a museum or at a major show.
land-rover-defender: The Defender is the direct heir of the original Land Rover, a tough, boxy vehicle built for farms, expeditions and rough ground. Its aluminium body panels do not rust like steel, but the steel chassis can. It is easy to repair in the field and has a huge community of owners. Check the chassis, bulkhead and rear crossmember carefully before buying.
austin-morris-mini: The Mini used a clever layout with the engine turned sideways, which left most of the car for people and luggage. It was tiny, cheap and surprisingly fun to drive, so it became popular with everyone from families to rally drivers. Check the sills, subframes and floors for rust, and remember that a cheap example can hide expensive repairs.
ferrari-f40: The F40 was the last Ferrari approved by Enzo Ferrari himself, and it was built as a raw, fast road car with very little comfort. It uses a twin-turbo V8 and a lightweight body. It is one of the most desired cars of its era and sits in the top tier of collector values. You are far more likely to see one in a picture than on an ordinary road.
lamborghini-countach: The Countach looked like a spaceship when it appeared, with sharp wedge lines and doors that swing upward. It became the poster car of a generation. It was hard to see out of and tiring to drive in town, but nobody bought it for comfort. Values are high today, and finding a well-documented car matters more than finding a cheap one.
honda-civic: The first-generation Civic arrived in the early 1970s as a small, efficient and well-built car at a time when fuel prices worried drivers. It helped Honda gain a strong name around the world. It is light and simple, with good fuel economy for its time. Early Civics are now scarce, so rust and missing parts are the main things to look out for.
toyota-land-cruiser-j40: The J40 Land Cruiser was built to go almost anywhere and to keep going for years. It has a strong chassis, simple controls and a reputation for reliability in hard conditions. Many are still used for work in remote areas. A well-kept one is a prized classic, but check the chassis and floor carefully, since rust can hide in several places.
hindustan-ambassador: The Ambassador was India’s best-known family and taxi car, based on an old British design. Its round shape and roomy interior made it easy to spot for decades. It was simple to repair, which suited busy roads and long working days. It is now a popular choice for nostalgic collectors in South Asia.
volkswagen-type-2-t1: The T1 bus, often called the Splitscreen, is one of the most loved vans in the world. Its rear engine and boxy body gave a lot of room for people and cargo. It became a symbol of travel and freedom. Prices are high, and rust in the body and the frame is the biggest worry, so a careful inspection is essential.
